title: From Genova to Gaza — Twenty-Five Years After the State Murder of Carlo Giuliani
author: Michael Leonardi
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/0-1-680x481.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/29/from-
genova-to-gaza-twenty-five-years-after-the-state-murder-of-carlo-giuliani/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/0-1-680x481.jpeg)  
On July 20, 2001, in the historic port city of Genova, the global ruling class
met behind the Red Zone while the Italian state showed the world exactly how
far it would go to protect them. Silvio Berlusconi played host to George W.
Bush, Tony Blair, and the rest of the G8. Outside, hundreds of thousands of
people from every corner of the planet had gathered to declare that another
world is possible. Among them was Carlo Giuliani, twenty-three years old, the
son of a CGIL trade-union militant, raised in a family that understood class
struggle as a living tradition.

What happened that day—and in the nights that followed—was not a “clash.” It
was a deliberate, coordinated suspension of the rule of law. Italian and
international police turned the streets into a war zone. Residents watched as
young people on their way to the beach were beaten in clouds of tear gas. Old
women and shopkeepers were attacked simply for being on their own streets. The
New World Order, cornered by a rising global movement, lashed out with the
ferocity of a wounded beast.

In the many conversations I have had over the years with Italians who were
there that week, a common thread always emerges. They speak of a sensation
that is almost impossible to describe unless you lived it: the sudden, total
suspension of the basic rights of individuals to protest, to gather, even to
walk the streets of their own city. The rule of law itself was set aside.
Police forces were given full reign to be as violent as they wanted, with the
open support of the Italian state and the world leaders gathered behind the
barriers. After the Battle of Seattle two years earlier — the uprising so
powerfully documented by Jeffrey St. Clair and Alexander Cockburn in 5 Days
That Shook the World — it felt as if a lesson had to be taught to the
international movement from below: a crushing blow delivered, fear
deliberately instilled. The message was unmistakable: this far, and no
further.

Carlo was one of those who fought back. When the Carabinieri jeep found itself
surrounded in Piazza Alimonda, he picked up a fire extinguisher. A shot rang
out from inside the vehicle. The bullet struck him in the head. Then the jeep
ran over his body—backwards and forwards. He was left to die on the pavement
while the leaders of the richest nations on earth continued their lunch.

I wrote about this on the tenth anniversary. The facts have not changed. The
photographs still show the gun pointed at Carlo’s head. The official
story—that the bullet “ricocheted”—was always a transparent cover-up. Mario
Placanica, the carabiniere who fired the shot, was never put on trial. He was
later promoted. The courts protected the chain of command.

That same night and the next, the state completed its lesson. Police stormed
the Armando Diaz school, where activists and independent journalists were
sleeping. What they did there has been described by one of their own as a
“Mexican butcher shop.” Bones were broken. Faces were smashed. Blood covered
the floors. Evidence was planted. Then the survivors were taken to the
Bolzaneto barracks, where the real torture chamber waited: beatings, forced
fascist songs, threats of rape, people forced to stand for hours in their own
urine and blood, medical staff who participated in the humiliation. This was
not rogue violence. This was policy. This was the Italian state, acting on
behalf of the global elite, teaching an entire generation what happens when
you challenge the order of capital and empire.

**Twenty-five years later, Genova remembered** :

On July 19, 2026, a national corteo of between five and ten thousand people
wound through the same streets. They started near the Diaz school, where a
banner proclaimed “Don’t clean up this blood – nessuno cancelli questo
sangue.” They moved through Via Tolemaide, site of the first major police
charges in 2001, past the headquarters of CasaPound—where activists of Genova
Antifascista erected a symbolic plasterboard wall declaring the area a “zona
denazificata”—and on to Piazza De Ferrari. Smoke filled the air. The central
slogan was clear and unapologetic: **“In ogni caso nessun rimorso”** — In any
case, no remorse.

The next day, July 20, the crowd returned to Piazza Alimonda itself. Organized
by the Comitato Piazza Carlo Giuliani under the motto “Chi non ha memoria non
ha futuro” (Whoever has no memory has no future), the gathering titled “Per
non dimentiCarlo” – To NotForgetCarlo filled the square with speeches, music,
and testimony. Flowers were laid at the memorial. An extinguisher was placed
on it — the same object Carlo had held in the final seconds of his life. At
17:27, the exact minute of the shooting, the piazza fell silent.

Elena Giuliani, Carlo’s sister, spoke with the clarity of someone who has
carried this wound for a quarter of a century. “I temi di allora sono ancora
tutti terribilmente, tragicamente presenti oggi,” she said—the themes of then
are still all terribly, tragically present today. Wars. The genocide in
Palestine. Climate collapse. Repression in the streets, in the prisons, in the
migrant detention centers, at the borders. She pointed to a recent George
Floyd style killing of a Moroccan immigrant named Abderrahim Fakir under
police restraint in Bologna and drew the straight line: “La repressione di
allora continua… Quello che noi chiedevamo allora è ancora valido ed
estremamente necessario.” The repression of then continues. What we asked for
then is still valid and extremely necessary. There was never a trial for her
brother’s killing. The case was dismissed quickly. She demanded institutional
responsibility and an end to the culture of impunity.

Participants unrolled a long white sheet across the square, transforming it
into a collective shroud. A text inspired by Paola Caridi’s work on Gaza was
read aloud, insisting that not a single name be forgotten. Activists from the
Freedom Flotilla Italia and Global Sumud Flotilla stood among them. The crowd
answered with the old chant, renewed for a new generation: **“Carlo è vivo e
lotta insieme a noi, le nostre idee non moriranno mai”** — Carlo is alive and
fights together with us; our ideas will never die. In that moment the memory
of Genova 2001 fused, without apology or hesitation, with the struggle against
the ongoing genocide in Palestine.

This is the sentiment of those who were there and those who have taken up the
torch. Not nostalgia. Not passive mourning. A living, political refusal. The
people who walked the corteo and filled Piazza Alimonda understand that the
suspension of the rule of law in July 2001 was not an aberration. It was a
demonstration of the permanent readiness of the capitalist state to use lethal
force and systematic torture when the movements of the exploited and the
oppressed grow too strong. The same logic that protected Bush, Blair, and
Berlusconi now protects the architects of the war on Gaza, the privatizers,
the climate destroyers, and the new fascist currents rising across Europe.

Carlo Giuliani was killed for resisting an unjust system that places profit
and empire above human life. His mother, Haidi Giuliani, has described him
simply and powerfully: **“Mio figlio, con la sua canottiera, è una figura
fragile che si ribella alla prepotenza”** — My son, with his tank top, is a
fragile figure who rebels against arrogance. In Palestine, that same system
has claimed thousands upon thousands of lives — children, journalists, medics,
students, entire families — whose only crime was to refuse disappearance, to
insist on remaining on their land, to resist. The fire extinguisher in Piazza
Alimonda and the rubble of Gaza are not separate stories. They are chapters of
the same book. The Italian state that ran Carlo over to protect the G8 is the
same state that today facilitates the arms shipments and political cover
enabling the slaughter. The movement that gathered in Genova this July
understood this clearly: the fight against capitalist globalization and the
fight for Palestinian liberation are one struggle.

The murder of Carlo Giuliani was never just about one young man and one
bullet. It was the moment the mask slipped. The global elite, meeting in
luxury while the planet burned and the poor were crushed, authorized the
Italian state to show us the price of resistance. They wanted us to be afraid.
They wanted the movement that had grown from Seattle to Genova to scatter and
die.

It did not die.

Twenty-five years later, the fire extinguisher still rests on the memorial in
Piazza Alimonda. The jeep still rolls over the body in the photographs. And
the people who were there — and the people who have come after — still refuse
the order that required Carlo’s death to protect itself. In Genova this year
they made the connection explicit: from Piazza Alimonda to Gaza, the same
system, the same resistance, the same demand that another world is possible.

Carlo lives because the struggle he died in continues. Palestine lives because
its people refuse to die. Another world is still possible. And the state that
killed him, and that enables the killing of so many others, still has blood on
its hands.
